newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam's Dak Lak hit by rains, bean moisture up.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's Dak Lak hit by rains, bean moisture up.

text.p: Torrential rains have again hit Vietnam's new robusta crop in Dak Lak province this week, rekindling fresh concerns about the quality of its beans and their moisture levels, coffee traders said on Thursday.

"It's started raining again in Dak Lak. This is bad news for the coffee in terms of its quality. One hasn't felt it as yet, but the situation has to be watched very closely," a trader in a European commodity house said.
The rains have hindered drying on smallholder farms that lack the equipment to do so, dealers said.

"If you're looking for coffee on nearby months, you may not be able to get it. They can't dry it fast enough," a trader in a Singapore-based coffee house said. "There may be a bit of a delay in the shipments." Dak Lak, located in Vietnam's highlands, produces two-thirds of the up to 270,000 tonnes of robusta beans exported by the country each year.
Traders said the rains have made transportation of coffee difficult to the main southern port of Ho Chi Minh city.
Moisture levels in the beans continue to hover at a high level of around 15-17 percent.
"You're having beans with a higher moisture content than buyers want. It should be shipped out at 13 percent," another trader said.
Selling remains brisk, however, with exports for November expected to reach around 20,000 tonnes.
"They've probably sold at least 25 percent of the crop. But the rains have definitely not helped," one trader said.
Indonesia robusta coffee trading continued to be thin with dealers just waiting for the new crop to be ready in March 1997, dealers said.
"What is left in terms of physical coffee in Indonesia is mainly pegged for domestic use," a dealer said.

Prices of Vietnam's Grade 2, 80 percent black and broken, robusta beans were priced by regional traders at about US$1,100 a tonne FOB Saigon port. Price quotes would hover within $20 of the figure, the dealers said.
Prices of Vietnam's Grade 2 last week were quoted in a range between $1,080-$1,150 a tonne FOB Saigon port, they said.
Indonesian Grade 4 robusta beans were quoted at $1,200-$1,250 a tonne FOB Panjang port, slightly lower than last week's price of about $1,250 a tonne, traders said.
LIFFE robusta coffee futures are expected to drift $5-$10 lower, following the lacklustre session of CSCE coffee futures in New York overnight.
"I think it's due $5 lower, especially after New York's weak close," a trader said.
The benchmark January contract closed $13 up at $1,449 a tonne in London after failing to clear the vital chart barrier at $1,450.
Singapore January robusta coffee futures closed at $1,338 a tonne on Wednesday after four tonnes were traded at $1,388.
Nine tonnes were traded on Tuesday.
Three tonnes of the January contract settled at $1,327 a tonne and six tonnes of the March contract settled $1,287 a tonne on the Singapore Commodity Exchange.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
